title: Can one chosen way of splitting prove two numbers co-prime?
description: Eighty and sixty three are each written as several products. One chosen product of each shows no shared factor, but the other products and the question marks show there may be more ways to split. Keeko doubts this and says the missing match is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: a missing match among a few chosen products does not prove two numbers co-prime, because another way of splitting may show a shared factor. Watch for students who stop at the first products that share nothing.

video_script.why: The child sees that a missing match among chosen products proves nothing, so a more careful way of checking is needed.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, eighty and sixty three, with the book's lists of products
video_script.anchor: the numbers eighty and sixty three with the book's lists of products and question marks
video_script.wrong_answer: the numbers are co-prime, because sixteen times five and nine times seven share no factor
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko picks sixteen times five and nine times seven, sees no common factor, and stops looking at other ways.
video_script.payoff_line: We cannot conclude that eighty and sixty three are co-prime from the products we chose

final_answer.value: No, a missing match among chosen products does not show that 80 and 63 are co-prime; a more systematic way is needed
final_answer.spoken: No, we cannot conclude it from the products we chose

names.{{NAME_3}}: the child who finds no match for fifty six and sixty three and wrongly says they are co-prime

maths_rules: 16 × 5 and 9 × 7 show the factors 16, 5, 9 and 7, and no factor is shared among them
a missing match among chosen products does not prove 80 and 63 are co-prime
more ways of splitting may exist, and each way names only two factors

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about eighty and sixty three.
<bookmark mark='eighty'/>The book writes eighty as forty times two, twenty times four, ten times eight and sixteen times five.
<bookmark mark='sixty'/>It writes sixty three as nine times seven and three times twenty one.
<bookmark mark='chosen'/>Take sixteen times five and nine times seven. These show no common factor.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we conclude that the two numbers are co-prime?

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the numbers are co-prime, because sixteen times five and nine times seven share no factor.
<bookmark mark='two'/>But those are only two of the many ways to split these numbers.
<bookmark mark='other'/>Eighty also splits as forty times two, and as twenty times four.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>A shared factor could hide in a way nobody tried, so a few chosen ways prove nothing.
